reply: It happened on Saturday when I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden and felt a twinge, but then I woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed, so that was three days ago. Since then, the pain is low down on the left side of my back and sometimes goes into my left buttock, and it gets worse when I bend or get out of a chair or by the evening, though it feels a bit better when I am lying still with a heat pack.

utterance:
Your examination shows tender, tight muscles in the left lower back, with normal leg strength, feeling and reflexes and no signs of a trapped nerve. This fits acute mechanical back pain, often called a back strain. There are no warning signs today suggesting a fracture, infection or cancer. Severe pain doesn't necessarily mean serious damage, and most episodes improve over days to a few weeks.

An MRI isn't needed now: it wouldn't change the treatment, and often shows ordinary disc changes in people without pain, which can lead to unnecessary worry or procedures. There is no indication for surgery. We would reconsider imaging if warning signs develop, or if you aren't improving over the next four to six weeks.

Just to confirm before recommending ibuprofen: are you taking any regular or over-the-counter medicines, including blood thinners, and are there any other allergies or heart problems?
reply: Are you sure we shouldn't do a scan just to be certain it isn't a slipped disc?

utterance: A scan can show a disc bulge, but it can't reliably tell us whether that is causing your pain. Your symptoms and normal nerve examination are reassuring: there's no evidence of a disc pressing on a nerve. Even if a disc is irritated, the initial treatment is the same and most people recover without surgery. I can't promise the exact structure causing the pain, but a scan now is unlikely to help you recover. We will review your progress rather than ignore it. Does that make sense?
reply: I suppose that makes sense, as long as we keep an eye on it if it doesn't get better.

utterance: Absolutely—we'll arrange a review in one week, sooner if you're getting worse. Can you confirm whether you take any other medicines, have any other allergies, or have heart disease?
reply: I don't have heart disease, and I am allergic to tramadol, which gives me vomiting and dizziness.

utterance: Are you currently taking any medicines other than the paracetamol you tried?
reply: No, I am not taking any other medicines.

dose: 200–400 mg with food, up to three times daily as needed; maximum 1200 mg per day

utterance:
For pain relief, try ibuprofen, one or two 200 mg tablets with food up to three times daily if needed, for up to three days. Use the lowest dose that helps, and don't exceed six tablets a day. Don't combine it with other anti-inflammatory painkillers such as naproxen or diclofenac. Keep hydrated, and don't take it if you're vomiting or dehydrated. Stop and seek advice if you get stomach pain; seek urgent help for black stools, vomiting blood, breathing difficulty or swelling. Paracetamol alone often doesn't help back pain, so you don't need to keep taking it if it hasn't helped. We won't use tramadol or other strong opioid medicines.

Keep moving gently rather than resting in bed or spending the day on the couch. Try short, frequent walks, gradually increasing what you can manage. Some discomfort with movement doesn't mean you're doing damage. Heat packs can help—wrap them to avoid burns. Avoid heavy lifting and repeated twisting for a few days, then gradually return to normal activities. At work, use a supportive chair, change position and take frequent standing or walking breaks. Temporary lighter duties or shorter hours are reasonable; you don't have to be completely pain-free to work. I can provide a certificate if needed. If movement remains difficult, a physiotherapist can help with a graded exercise plan.

Go straight to emergency if you develop difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around your genitals or bottom, or new significant leg weakness. Seek urgent review for fever, feeling very unwell, or rapidly worsening or constant pain that isn't eased by rest. Let's review in a week to check pain, movement and medication needs; come back sooner if the pain isn't manageable. How does this plan sound?
reply: That makes sense, and I appreciate you taking the time to explain it all properly.

awards.label: Correct diagnosis: Acute non-specific low back pain
